opus-5.5.text:
I think there's some truth to it, but it's often overstated. What fine-tuning a small model does really well is capture the surface behavior of a larger model. If you take a seven-billion-parameter model and train it on outputs from a much stronger system, it learns the style, the formatting, the tone of a helpful assistant, and on the kinds of prompts people casually try, it can look remarkably close. But when you probe deeper, on harder reasoning, on multi-step problems, on factual knowledge in the long tail, or on situations that are a bit out of distribution, the gap tends to show up pretty quickly. A lot of the underlying capability seems to come from pretraining, from scale and data, and a small amount of fine-tuning doesn't magically add that knowledge. It mostly teaches the model how to present what it already has.

Part of the issue is evaluation. Many of the comparisons rely on things like having another model or crowd workers judge which answer they prefer, and those judgments are heavily influenced by fluency and confidence rather than correctness. So you can get a model that sounds just as good while being wrong more often.

That said, I don't want to dismiss the open-source work, because it's been hugely valuable. It shows that for narrow, well-defined tasks, a smaller specialized model can be very competitive and much cheaper to run. And it lets researchers like me actually experiment with these systems, understand how they work, and try new ideas, which you can't do with a closed API. So I'd say the right framing is: small fine-tuned models can match large models on specific things, but matching them in general capability is a much harder claim, and I don't think the evidence supports it yet.

r001.rationale: The response says small fine-tuned models can match large models on specific tasks, but that general capability matching is a much harder claim and the evidence does not support it.

r002.rationale: The response does not recommend that the open-source community use additional GPUs to improve model performance.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there's some truth to it and also some real misunderstanding wrapped up in the same claim. The truth is that fine-tuning is remarkably effective at eliciting behaviors that are already latent in a model. If you take a smaller open model and fine-tune it on a few thousand high-quality instruction-following examples, often distilled from a larger model, it will look dramatically better on the kinds of things people tend to check first: it'll follow the format, it'll sound polished, it'll do well on a chat-style benchmark or a human preference comparison. So on the surface, yes, it can look like you've closed most of the gap very cheaply.

Where I get more skeptical is when you push on what that fine-tuning actually changed. My read is that fine-tuning mostly teaches the model a style and an interface. It doesn't put new knowledge or new reasoning capability into the weights to any significant degree. Those come from pretraining, from scale and from data. So when you move away from the surface and look at things like multi-step reasoning, factual coverage in the long tail, coding tasks that require really holding a lot of context, or robustness when the input is a bit out of distribution, the small models tend to fall off much harder than the leading models do. The gap was never really in the formatting, it was in the underlying capability, and a small amount of supervised data doesn't fix that.

There's also an evaluation issue here. A lot of the early claims were based on having a strong model judge the outputs, and those judges are quite biased toward answers that look confident and well-structured. A model that imitates the style of GPT-4 will score well with a GPT-4 judge even if it's wrong more often. When people have done more careful evaluations, where you actually check correctness, the "matches the leading model" story has usually shrunk to "matches on easy things, lags on hard things."

That said, I don't want to be dismissive, because I think the practical lesson is actually important. For many real applications, you don't need the frontier model. If your task is narrow and well-specified, a small fine-tuned model can be good enough, far cheaper, and you can run it yourself. And from a research standpoint, the fact that so little data is needed to unlock these behaviors tells us something interesting about how much is already there after pretraining. So I'd frame it less as "small models can match big models" and more as "fine-tuning is cheap and powerful at shaping behavior, but capability still comes from scale, and we should be honest about measuring the difference."

r001.rationale: The response says small fine-tuned models can appear to close the gap on easy or surface-level tasks but fall behind leading models on harder tasks, so the broad matching claim overstates their performance.

r002.rationale: The response does not recommend that the open-source community use additional GPUs to improve model performance.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by “match.” If you have a very specific task and you fine-tune a small model on examples of that task, it can be competitive with a much larger model. That’s exciting, because you may not need a large, expensive model for every application.

But matching performance on a particular benchmark is different from matching the breadth of a leading model. Does it still work when you change the question, or ask it to do something outside the fine-tuning distribution? That’s where I’d want to look more carefully. So I think these results can be valuable, but the scope of the claim matters.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes task-specific benchmark performance from matching a leading model’s broader capabilities, but it does not state that actual performance falls short of the community’s claims.

r002.rationale: The response makes no recommendation for the open-source community to use additional GPUs to improve performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by “match.” If you have a very specific task and you fine-tune a small model on examples from that task, it can be very competitive with a much larger model. That’s exciting, because you may not need a huge model for every application.

But that’s different from matching the larger model’s general capabilities. If you change the task or ask something outside the fine-tuning distribution, the gap can show up again. So I’d want to know how narrow the evaluation is and whether the improvement carries over to new settings. Strong performance on one benchmark is useful, but it doesn’t establish that the models are equivalent.
